Socialist republic (pop. over 102 million) on the eastern edge of [[Mainland Southeast Asia]]. Its area is about 331,000 sq km, and it is the world's 16th-most populous country. Vietnam is bordered by China to the north and by Laos and Cambodia to the west, and it lies along the Gulf of Thailand and the South China Sea. The capital is [[Hanoi]]; the largest city is [[Ho Chi Minh City]]. The Kinh people form the large majority of the population.

States arose in the first millennium BC on the Red River Delta. The [[Han dynasty]] annexed northern and central Vietnam, which remained under Chinese rule from 111 BC until the first dynasty emerged in 939. Successive monarchical dynasties absorbed Chinese influences through Confucianism and Buddhism and expanded south to the Mekong Delta, conquering Champa. During most of the 17th and 18th centuries the country was effectively divided into two domains, Đàng Trong and Đàng Ngoài. The Nguyễn, the last imperial dynasty, surrendered to France in 1883, and in 1887 the territory was integrated into [[French Indochina]] as three separate regions. The communist-led Viet Minh declared independence in 1945. France was defeated in the [[First Indochina War]] in 1954, and the country was divided in two. The [[Vietnam War]] followed between communist North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, and South Vietnam, supported by the United States. After the North Vietnamese victory in 1975, the country reunified in 1976 under the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV).

A planned economy, a Western trade embargo, and wars with Cambodia and China crippled the country until the CPV launched reforms in 1986 that created a socialist-oriented market economy. Vietnam is now an upper-middle-income economy and a one-party state in which the constitution designates the CPV as the leading force. Observers cite corruption, censorship, environmental problems, restrictions on political pluralism and expression, and a poor human rights record. Vietnam belongs to [[ASEAN]], APEC, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the WTO, and has held a seat on the UN Security Council twice.

Period of the [[Middle Ages]], about 800–1050, of large-scale raiding, colonizing, conquest, and trading by Norsemen, known as [[Vikings]]. The term covers Scandinavia and any place significantly settled by Scandinavians in the period. Few of them were Vikings in the sense of engaging in piracy. Traditional accounts place the beginning at the attack of June 8, 793, that destroyed the abbey on Lindisfarne, off Northumberland, and the end at the defeat of the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada at the [[Battle of Stamford Bridge]] in 1066. The historian Judith Jesch has argued that the start can be pushed back to 700–750.

Voyaging from Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, the Norse settled in the British Isles, Ireland, the Faroe Islands, [[Iceland]], Greenland, [[Normandy]], and the Baltic coast, and along the Dnieper and Volga trade routes, where they were known as Varangians. They briefly settled in Newfoundland, becoming the first Europeans to reach North America; the voyage is dated to 1021. They founded the Kingdom of the Isles, Orkney, York and the Danelaw, Dublin, Normandy, and [[Kievan Rus']]. In the 11th century the Norse homelands were unified into larger kingdoms, and the short-lived North Sea Empire of [[Cnut]] included large parts of Scandinavia and Britain. Trade carried furs, amber, walrus ivory, and iron to the Byzantine Empire and Islamic caliphates.

Proposed causes of expansion include wealthy towns and monasteries overseas, weak kingdoms, overpopulation, lack of good farmland, political strife arising from the unification of Norway, Carolingian expansion, and innovations in sailing. By the mid-11th century the adoption of Christianity and integration into feudal Europe had diminished a distinct Viking identity.

Knowledge comes largely from texts written by those the Vikings encountered, from archaeology, and from later sources such as the Icelandic [[Saga|sagas]]. Enemies portrayed Vikings as violent, and by the late 18th century the age was widely regarded as barbaric. Scholars outside Scandinavia began reassessing it in the 1890s, recognizing the Vikings' artistry, technological skills, and seamanship.

[[Human settlement]] larger than a hamlet but smaller than a [[Town|town]], with dwellings fairly close together rather than dispersed across the landscape. Some geographers describe villages as having between 500 and 2,500 inhabitants. Villages are often located in [[Rural area|rural areas]], though the term "urban village" is also applied to certain urban neighborhoods. They are normally permanent, but transient villages also exist.

Villages originated with the shift from nomadic hunter-gatherer life to sedentary life about 12,000 years ago in the Levant, where groups such as the Natufians built permanent stone houses. They were long a usual form of community for societies practicing [[Subsistence agriculture|subsistence agriculture]] and for some non-agricultural societies. Homes were grouped for sociability and defense, with the surrounding land farmed; traditional fishing villages lay next to fishing grounds. In Great Britain, a hamlet earned the right to be called a village when it built a church. The [[Industrial Revolution]] drew people to mills and factories and turned many villages into towns and cities, and [[Urbanization|urbanization]] continues.

Usage and administrative status vary widely. In Afghanistan the *deh* is a mid-size settlement, larger than the *qala* (hamlet) and smaller than the *shār* (town). In [[India]], 69% of the population (around 833 million people) lived in villages at the 2011 census, which counted 649,481 villages; 236,004 had fewer than 500 inhabitants and 3,976 had 10,000 or more. About 61% of Pakistanis live in rural areas, according to the 2023 census. In Kazakhstan, 42.7% of citizens (7.5 million people) lived in 8172 villages (*auyl*) in 2009. In mainland China and Taiwan, villages are divisions under townships or towns. Japan has 183 villages, a number that is decreasing through mergers and status elevation. In Southeast Asia the *kampung* (also *kampong*) is the traditional village; in Brunei it is the lowest-level subdivision, headed by a village head. In [[Indonesia]], villages are called *kampung* or *desa*, or *kelurahan* where urban in function. A *desa* is administered by customary law (*adat*), and its head is elected by the local community.

Dutch Post-Impressionist painter. In just over a decade he created about 2,100 artworks, including around 860 oil paintings, most of them in the last two years of his life. They include landscapes, still lifes, portraits, and self-portraits, characterized by bold colors and dramatic, expressive brushwork that contributed to the foundations of modern art.

Born into an upper-middle-class family in Zundert, he worked as an art dealer, became depressed after a transfer to London, and spent time as a Protestant missionary in southern Belgium. He took up painting in 1881. His younger brother Theo, an art dealer, supported him financially, and their long correspondence, with more than 600 letters from Vincent to Theo, is the most comprehensive source on his thought and methods. His early works, mostly still lifes and depictions of peasant laborers, show few signs of the vivid color of his later work. In 1886 he moved to Paris, where he met members of the [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]], including Émile Bernard and [[Paul Gauguin]]. His palette brightened, and his style became fully realized in Arles in 1888, where he painted series of olive trees, wheat fields, and sunflowers.

Van Gogh suffered from psychotic episodes and delusions and drank heavily. His friendship with Gauguin ended after a confrontation, when he severed part of his own left ear. He spent time in psychiatric hospitals, including at Saint-Rémy, where he painted *The Starry Night* (1889). He then moved to Auvers-sur-Oise, near Paris, and came under the care of Paul Gachet. In 1890 he shot himself in the chest with a revolver and died two days later.

Largely unsuccessful in his lifetime, with only one well-documented sale, he became famous after his death. His sister-in-law Johanna van Gogh-Bonger arranged publication of the letters in 1906, 1913, and 1914. His reputation grew in the early 20th century as the Fauves and German [[Expressionism|Expressionists]] incorporated elements of his style, and he is now widely seen as a pioneer of [[Modern art|modern art]].

Use of physical force or power, threatened or actual, to cause harm to living beings. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines it as "the intentional use of physical force or power, threatened or actual, against oneself, another person, or against a group or community, which either results in or has a high likelihood of resulting in injury, death, psychological harm, maldevelopment, or deprivation," and recognizes the need to include violence that does not result in injury or death.

The WHO divides violence into three categories: self-directed, interpersonal, and collective. Violence can alternatively be classified as instrumental or hostile. Self-directed violence includes suicidal behavior and [[Self-harm|self-harm]]. Collective violence is the instrumental use of violence by members of a group against another group to achieve political, economic, or social objectives; its most extreme form is [[War|war]]. Related concepts include economic violence, slow violence (gradual and often invisible, working through degradation and pollution), and structural violence, in which a social structure or institution harms people by preventing them from meeting basic needs or rights.

Interpersonal violence can be classified by type of abuse, by location, or by age disparity between the people involved. Intimate partner violence, also called [[Domestic violence|domestic violence]], involves physical, sexual, and emotional violence by a partner or ex-partner. Males can be victims, but it disproportionately affects females. The prevention strategy with the best evidence of effectiveness is school-based programming for adolescents to prevent dating violence.

Violence against children covers all forms of violence against people under 18, including maltreatment and neglect by parents, caregivers, peers, or strangers. There are no reliable global estimates of its prevalence. Approximately 20% of women and 5–10% of men report being sexually abused as children, and 25–50% of all children report physical abuse. Childhood trauma raises the risk of mental illness, suicide, substance abuse, and chronic disease.

Intentional [[Homicide|homicide]], armed conflict, and terrorism together caused approximately 556,000 deaths a year on average between 2019 and 2021, of which about 440,000 were homicides. Explanations range from evolutionary accounts of aggression to social and structural ones.

Roman poet of the Augustan period, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro; also spelled Vergil. Born in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, to parents of modest means, he composed three of the most famous poems in [[Latin literature]]: the *Eclogues* (or *Bucolics*), the *Georgics*, and the epic *[[Aeneid]]*. Some minor poems collected in the *Appendix Vergiliana* were attributed to him in antiquity, but modern scholars regard most as spurious.

The *Eclogues* are ten pastoral poems modeled on Theocritus, exploring rural life, love, and politics, with allusions to land confiscations during the civil wars. The *Georgics*, composed around 29 BC, is a didactic poem in four books on agriculture, viticulture, animal husbandry, and beekeeping. The *Aeneid*, in twelve books and unfinished at his death, recounts the Trojan hero Aeneas's voyage from the ruins of [[Troy]] to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. It blends Homeric influences with a providential narrative that supported the regime of [[Augustus]]; modern readers also see in it a reckoning with the costs of founding a civilization, including war, loss, and moral ambiguity. Virgil was supported by patrons such as Maecenas and was close to [[Horace]]. According to tradition, he asked on his deathbed at Brundisium that the *Aeneid* be burned, but his executors Varius and Tucca published it with minimal changes.

Biographical details come from later ancient *vitae* by Donatus, Servius, and others, which draw largely on a lost work by Suetonius. Some of their evidence relies on allegorizing and on inferences from his poetry, so details of his life are considered problematic. A medieval legend that Virgil was a magician probably arose from confusion over the name of his mother's family, Magius.

Virgil was acclaimed in his lifetime and replaced Ennius as a standard school text. He remained the most popular Latin poet through late antiquity, the [[Middle Ages]], and early modernity. In Dante's [[Divine Comedy]] he appears as the author's guide through Hell and Purgatory. [[T. S. Eliot]] began his lecture "What Is a Classic?" by asserting that any definition of a classic must reckon with Virgil.

Submicroscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of an organism. Viruses infect all life forms, from animals and plants to bacteria and archaea, and are found in almost every ecosystem on Earth. They are the most numerous type of biological entity. The first virus discovered, in the 1890s, was the [[Tobacco mosaic virus|tobacco mosaic virus]]; since then more than 16,000 of the millions of virus species have been described in detail. The study of viruses is virology, a subspecialty of [[Microbiology|microbiology]].

Outside a host cell, a virus exists as a viral particle, or virion, consisting of genetic material (long molecules of [[DNA]] or [[RNA]]); a protein coat, the capsid; and in some cases an outer envelope of lipids. Shapes range from simple helical and icosahedral forms to more complex structures. Most virions are too small to be seen with an optical microscope, and are one-hundredth the size of most bacteria. Inside an infected cell, the host is often forced to produce thousands of copies of the original virus.

The origins of viruses are unclear, since they do not form fossils. Hypotheses include descent from small parasitic cells that lost unneeded genes, and escape of DNA or RNA from larger organisms, such as from [[Plasmid|plasmids]]. Viruses are an important means of horizontal gene transfer. Some biologists consider them a life form because they carry genetic material, reproduce, and evolve through natural selection, though they lack characteristics such as cell structure; they have been described as "organisms at the edge of life."

Transmission routes include vectors such as aphids and blood-sucking insects; coughing and sneezing, as with influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2, chickenpox, smallpox, and measles; the faecal–oral route, as with norovirus and rotavirus; and sexual contact and infected blood, as with HIV. The variety of cells a virus can infect is its host range. Animal immune responses usually eliminate the infection, and [[Vaccine|vaccines]] produce immunity artificially. Some viruses evade these responses and cause chronic infections. Around 100 antiviral drugs or combinations are used worldwide.

Art forms perceived chiefly through sight, including [[Painting|painting]], drawing, printmaking, sculpture, ceramics, photography, video, filmmaking, design, crafts, and [[Architecture|architecture]]. The applied arts, such as industrial, graphic, fashion, and interior design and decorative art, are also included, and disciplines such as performing arts, conceptual art, and textile arts involve aspects of the visual arts.

Current usage covers fine art as well as applied arts and crafts, but this was not always so. Before the [[Arts and Crafts movement]] at the turn of the 20th century, the term "artist" had for centuries often been restricted to practitioners of the fine arts such as painting and sculpture, and art schools maintained that a craftsperson could not be considered an artist. The Arts and Crafts movement challenged this by valuing vernacular forms as highly as "high" ones. Both Western and East Asian art have tended to privilege painting, and to a lesser degree sculpture, as the arts that rely most on imagination and are furthest removed from manual labor. In Chinese painting, the valued "scholar-painting" was in theory practiced by gentleman amateurs.

Training began as apprentice and workshop systems, typically lasting 2 to 6 years. In many European and North American nations, academies grew into universities and institutes, while education has followed different paths elsewhere: some Sub-Saharan African nations have de-prioritized art in primary curricula, and Singapore has focused resources on digital visual arts. Museums and galleries serve as informal education.

Drawing makes a two-dimensional image by marking a surface with tools such as graphite pencils, pen and ink, charcoal, pastels, and markers, or with digital tools. Its main techniques include line drawing, hatching, crosshatching, shading, stippling, and blending. Upper Paleolithic art includes figurative art beginning at least 40,000 years ago, and cave sites include Lascaux in France, Altamira in Spain, Maros in Sulawesi, and Gabarnmung in Australia. Ancient Egyptians drew in ink on potsherds and limestone ostraca, and Greek vase painting developed black-figure pottery in the 6th century BC. With paper brought by Islamic traders from China, drawing on paper increased in the Middle East and Europe in the 14th century, and artists such as Raphael, Michelangelo, and [[Leonardo da Vinci]] treated it as an art in its own right rather than a preparatory stage.

Painting applies pigments suspended in a medium with a binder to a surface such as walls, canvas, or paper. The earliest evidence is natural pigments of ochre, chalk, and charcoal applied to stone; tools for processing pigments for body painting date to about 200,000 years ago in Zambia, and cave paintings to at least 50,000 years ago. Later traditions developed fresco, tempera (egg yolk, animal glue, or milk), and encaustic (hot wax), while ink wash painting became a major East Asian tradition. Oil paint on wood panels, later on stretched canvas, permitted shading and glazing and the use of chiaroscuro. In the 19th century the box easel and collapsible paint tube allowed *plein air* painting outdoors.

Movements since the Renaissance include Baroque, Rococo, Neoclassicism, Romanticism, Impressionism, Cubism, Abstract Expressionism, and Pop Art. Contemporary practice often incorporates performance, installation, and new media.

Organic molecules, or sets of closely related molecules called vitamers, essential in small quantities to an organism for proper [[Metabolism|metabolic]] function. They cannot be synthesized in sufficient quantities for survival and must be obtained through consumption. [[Vitamin C]], for example, is synthesized by some species but not others, and is a vitamin only for the latter. Most vitamins are groups of vitamers; vitamin E has eight, four tocopherols and four tocotrienols. The other essential nutrients are minerals, essential fatty acids, essential amino acids, and choline.

Major health organizations list thirteen vitamins: the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, and the water-soluble vitamin C and eight B vitamins. Their functions are diverse. Vitamin A regulates cell and tissue growth and differentiation. [[Vitamin D]] acts like a hormone, regulating mineral metabolism for bones and other organs. The B complex vitamins serve as [[Enzyme|enzyme]] cofactors or their precursors. Vitamins C and E are antioxidants, and vitamin K aids blood clotting. Both deficiency and excess can cause illness. In otherwise healthy people there is little evidence that supplements protect against heart disease or cancer.

All vitamins were discovered between the 1900s and 1930s, but the effects of deficiency were recognized earlier. Ancient Egyptians knew that feeding liver could help night blindness, now known to result from vitamin A deficiency. Long ocean voyages made [[Scurvy|scurvy]] common among ships' crews. In 1747 the Scottish surgeon James Lind ran a controlled experiment on 12 sailors showing that citrus foods helped prevent it, and his *Treatise on the Scurvy* (1753) recommended lemons and limes, which the British [[Royal Navy]] adopted. Limes from the West Indies later replaced lemons and proved much lower in vitamin C, so Arctic expeditions were still plagued by scurvy. In 1884 Takaki Kanehiro of the Imperial Japanese Navy observed that beriberi was endemic among low-ranking crew who ate mostly rice, but not among officers with a Western-style diet.

Casimir Funk and Max Nierenstein coined "vitamine" in 1912 from "vital amine." In 1920 Jack Cecil Drummond proposed dropping the final "e," because not all vitamins were amines. Commercial vitamin tablets appeared in 1935, followed in the 1950s by mass-produced supplements. Governments have mandated adding some vitamins to staple foods such as flour or milk, and folic acid supplementation in pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

Vent or fissure in the crust of a planetary-mass object through which hot lava, volcanic ash, and gases escape from a [[Magma chamber|magma chamber]] below. On Earth, volcanoes lie mostly where tectonic plates diverge or converge, and because most plate boundaries are underwater, most volcanoes are too. The word derives from Vulcano, an island in the Aeolian Islands of Italy, named for Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.

According to [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]], most volcanic activity takes place along plate boundaries. At divergent boundaries such as the [[Mid-Atlantic Ridge]], rising mantle rock partly melts and creates new oceanic crust; these volcanoes are usually nonexplosive. Where a ridge rises above sea level, volcanic islands such as [[Iceland]] form. At convergent boundaries, one plate subducts beneath another, and water released from it lowers the melting temperature of the overlying mantle, producing magma that is extremely viscous because of its high silica content. These volcanoes cause violent eruptions and form volcanic arcs, as around the Pacific [[Ring of Fire]], which holds about 75% of the world's active volcanoes. Volcanoes also form where the crust stretches and thins, as in the East African Rift, and above hotspots, thought to be fed by mantle plumes rising from 3,000 km deep, as in the Hawaiian island chain. Volcanoes are usually not created at transform boundaries.

By frequency of eruption, volcanoes are called active, dormant, or extinct. Dormant volcanoes have not erupted since roughly the start of the [[Holocene]], about 12,000 years ago, but may erupt again. About 1,350 potentially active volcanoes exist on land, around 500 of which have erupted in historical times. Principal types include shield volcanoes, broad and gently sloping, such as [[Mauna Loa]]; stratovolcanoes, steep cones of alternating lava and pyroclastic layers, such as [[Mount Fuji]]; cinder cones; and lava domes.

Hazards include lava flows, pyroclastic flows, ash falls that disrupt air travel, and lahars, or volcanic mudflows. Large eruptions can cool the troposphere as ash and droplets of sulfuric acid obscure the Sun, and historically have been followed by volcanic winters that caused catastrophic famines. Volcanic soils support dense populations, and volcanoes supply geothermal energy, pumice, and sulfur. Venus has very numerous volcanoes, and Mars has significant ones. A 2009 paper proposed a definition broad enough to include cryovolcanism on other planets and moons.
